items.q: Which claim about the data is best supported?
options: Molar mass cannot account for the boiling points, because the three are nearly equal in mass yet differ by about 98 °C.
Molar mass accounts for the boiling points, because 1-propanol is the heaviest and boils highest of the three compounds.
Electron count accounts for the boiling points, because acetone has the fewest electrons and boils the lowest of the three.
Boiling point falls as molar mass rises, because heavier molecules move more slowly and escape the liquid less often.

items.q: Why does acetone boil about 57 °C higher than butane?
options: Acetone is polar, so dipole-dipole forces add to its dispersion forces; butane is nonpolar and has dispersion forces alone.
Acetone forms hydrogen bonds between its molecules through the lone pairs on its oxygen atom, which butane, a molecule with no oxygen, lacks.
Acetone has more electrons than butane, so its London dispersion forces are much stronger than the dispersion forces between butane molecules.
Boiling acetone breaks its strong C=O double bond, which takes more energy than breaking the C–C bonds in butane.

items.q: Which attractions act between molecules of liquid 1-propanol? Select all that apply.
options: London dispersion forces
Dipole-dipole forces
Hydrogen bonds
Ion-dipole forces
Covalent bonds between neighboring molecules

items.q: A classmate writes: "1-Propanol boils highest because boiling breaks its O–H bonds, which are strong." What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Boiling separates whole molecules from each other; the O–H covalent bonds stay intact and the vapor is still 1-propanol.
O–H bonds are weaker than C–H bonds, so breaking them would lower the boiling point rather than raise it.
The O–H bonds do break on boiling, but the energy needed is too small to change the boiling point.
Hydrogen bonds are a kind of covalent bond, so the classmate has named the right bond with the wrong name.

items.q: Ethylene glycol, HOCH₂CH₂OH (62.07 g/mol), has two O–H groups per molecule. How would its boiling point most likely compare with that of 1-propanol?
options: Higher, because each molecule can form more hydrogen bonds with its neighbors.
Lower, because it has two oxygen atoms, which makes the molecule less polarizable.
About the same, because the two molar masses differ by just 2 g/mol, so their attractions are about equal.
Lower, because its two O–H groups cancel each other's dipoles and leave it nonpolar.

items.q: Which explanation accounts for the rise in boiling point from F₂ to I₂?
options: More electrons in larger electron clouds make the molecules more polarizable, so dispersion forces grow stronger.
Each molecule down the group is more polar than the one above it, so the dipole-dipole forces between neighboring molecules grow stronger.
The covalent bond inside each molecule grows stronger down the group, so more energy is needed to boil it.
Heavier molecules are pulled down by gravity more strongly, so they need more energy to escape as a gas.

items.q: At room temperature (about 22 °C), which of the halogens in the table is a liquid?
options: Br₂
Cl₂
I₂
F₂

items.q: F₂ and Ar have the same number of electrons and boil only 2 °C apart. What does this pair best show?
options: Dispersion strength depends on the number of electrons rather than on whether the particle is a molecule or an atom.
Diatomic molecules attract each other more weakly than single atoms of the same element group.
The boiling point of a nonpolar substance is set by its molar mass, and the two molar masses are close enough to count as the same.
Noble gas atoms form hydrogen bonds with each other, which makes up for their small atomic size.

items.q: Xenon has 54 electrons. Based on the table, which is the most reasonable boiling point for xenon?
Which labeled dashed lines correctly show hydrogen bonds? Select all that apply.
options: W
X
Y
Z

items.q: Why can line Y not be a hydrogen bond?
options: It connects two partially negative oxygen atoms, which repel each other, and it has no H atom bridging them.
It is drawn too long; a hydrogen bond forms between atoms that touch in a diagram.
It connects two different molecules, and a hydrogen bond forms between atoms of one molecule.
Oxygen atoms are too large to take part in hydrogen bonds, unlike nitrogen and fluorine atoms, which are smaller.

items.q: When this sample of water boils, which interactions are overcome?
options: Hydrogen bonds such as W and X; the O–H bonds inside each molecule stay intact.
The O–H covalent bonds inside each molecule, which releases hydrogen and oxygen atoms into the vapor.
Both the hydrogen bonds and the O–H covalent bonds, since boiling adds a great deal of energy.
Neither kind: boiling speeds up the molecules, but the attractions between them stay as they were in the liquid.

items.q: How could the top-right molecule be redrawn so that line Z became a hydrogen bond?
options: Turn it so that its O atom, with its lone pairs, faces the H at the left end of line Z.
Turn it so that both of its H atoms point straight up, away from the top-left molecule.
Move it farther from the top-left molecule so that the two H atoms stop repelling.
Replace one of its H atoms with a second O atom so the line joins H to O inside one molecule.

items.q: For the group 14 hydrides, how does boiling point change from period 2 to period 5?
options: It rises steadily, from −162 °C to −52 °C.
It falls steadily, from −52 °C to −162 °C.
It falls from period 2 to period 3, then rises.
It stays within a few degrees of −110 °C.

items.q: Why do the group 14 hydrides show no high point at period 2, while groups 15 and 16 do?
options: CH₄ has no H bonded to N, O or F, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds; NH₃ and H₂O can.
CH₄ is the heaviest molecule in its group, which keeps its boiling point near the others.
CH₄ has a strong polar C–H bond that cancels the hydrogen bonds between its molecules.
Carbon has more electrons than nitrogen or oxygen, so its hydride has the strongest dispersion forces.

items.q: H₂S, H₂Se and H₂Te are all polar. Which statement best explains why their boiling points rise from H₂S to H₂Te?
options: Down the group the molecules have more electrons, so dispersion forces grow and outweigh small changes in polarity.
Down the group the molecules form more hydrogen bonds, because S, Se and Te each have two lone pairs that can accept them.
Down the group the molecules become more polar, because Te is more electronegative than S.
Down the group the H–X covalent bonds get stronger and longer, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules from one another.

items.q: Water (10 electrons) boils at 100 °C, but H₂Te (54 electrons) boils at −2 °C. A student says this shows dispersion forces do not depend on electron count. Which response is best?
options: H₂Te does have stronger dispersion forces, but water's hydrogen bonds add an attraction large enough to outweigh that difference.
The student is right: water has fewer electrons but stronger dispersion forces because its molecules are smaller.
H₂Te boils lower because its covalent bonds are weaker, so its molecules fall apart sooner when heated.
Water boils higher because it is heavier per molecule than H₂Te, which offsets its smaller electron count.

items.q: Pentane (a five-carbon chain) boils at 36 °C. Its isomer 2,2-dimethylpropane, a compact, nearly spherical molecule with the same formula, boils at 10 °C. Which explanation is best?
options: The chains touch each other over a larger surface, so the dispersion attractions between them are stronger.
The chain molecules have more electrons, so they are more polarizable than the compact molecules.
The chain molecules are polar because their ends differ, while the compact, symmetric molecules are nonpolar and have no dipole.
The compact molecules have a larger molar mass, which lets them escape the liquid more easily.

items.q: Which attraction acts between the particles of every substance?
options: London dispersion forces
Dipole-dipole forces
Hydrogen bonds
Ion-dipole forces

items.q: Which pure substances form hydrogen bonds between their own molecules? Select all that apply.
options: CH₃OH (methanol)
CH₃OCH₃ (dimethyl ether)
CH₃F (fluoromethane)
HCl (hydrogen chloride)
NH₃ (ammonia)

items.q: Which substance has the higher boiling point, ICl (162.4 g/mol) or Br₂ (159.8 g/mol), and why?
options: ICl, because it is polar and has dipole-dipole forces in addition to dispersion forces of similar strength.
Br₂, because its molecules are made of one element, so the electron clouds are more even and attract more.
ICl, because it has the larger molar mass, and molar mass alone sets the boiling point of a substance.
They boil at the same temperature, because both molecules contain exactly 70 electrons each.

items.q: Put these substances in order of boiling point, lowest first.
options: CH₄ (methane)
C₃H₈ (propane)
CH₃OCH₃ (dimethyl ether)
CH₃CH₂OH (ethanol)

items.q: What is a hydrogen bond?
options: An attraction between an H atom bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F of another molecule
A covalent bond between a hydrogen atom and any other atom inside one molecule
An attraction between two hydrogen atoms on neighboring molecules that share a pair of electrons between them
An attraction between any H atom and the most electronegative atom of a neighboring molecule

items.q: Octane, C₈H₁₈ (66 electrons, nonpolar), boils at 126 °C, higher than water at 100 °C. Which statement best explains this?
options: Octane's large, polarizable electron cloud and long contact area give dispersion forces that add up to more than water's attractions.
Octane forms hydrogen bonds through its 18 H atoms, many more than the two H atoms that each water molecule can offer to its neighbors.
Octane is a polar molecule because it has so many C–H bonds, each adding a small dipole.
Octane boils higher because more of its 25 covalent bonds have to break before the liquid can turn into a vapor.

items.q: Which solid is most likely a molecular solid?
options: W
X
Y
Z

items.q: Which observation best shows that solid W is ionic rather than metallic?
options: W conducts when melted but not as a solid.
W melts at 801 °C, which is higher than the melting points of the common metals found in the periodic table, such as copper and iron.
W is white, while metals have a shiny, silvery color that reflects light from their surfaces.
W is hard, while metals are soft enough to be cut with a knife at room temperature.

items.q: Which explanation accounts for solid Y's very high melting point and lack of conductivity?
options: Its atoms form one covalent network, so melting breaks covalent bonds and no charges can move.
Its molecules form many hydrogen bonds to each other, which are strong enough to keep it solid at 1,700 °C.
Its ions are held by very strong ionic bonds, and ions do not carry a current even when the solid has melted into a liquid.
It is a metal whose electrons are held so tightly that they stay put, which raises the melting point.

items.q: When solid Z is hammered, it flattens instead of shattering. Which particle-level explanation fits?
options: Layers of cations slide while the electron sea keeps holding them together.
Hammering breaks the covalent bonds between atoms, and new covalent bonds form in the new shape.
Like-charged ions are pushed next to each other, and their repulsion pushes the layers apart.
The intermolecular forces between its molecules are weak, so the molecules move apart and spread out.

items.q: A fifth solid, V, melts at 186 °C and does not conduct when melted. Which conclusions are supported? Select all that apply.
options: V is a molecular solid.
V's covalent bonds break when it melts.
V contains no free ions or electrons.
V is an ionic solid with small ions.

items.q: Which box shows a solid that conducts electricity as a solid?
options: Box 1
Box 2
Box 3
Box 4

items.q: Which box best represents solid iodine, I₂?
options: Box 1
Box 2
Box 3
Box 4

items.q: The substance in box 1 melts far lower than the substance in box 3. Which reasoning is correct?
options: Melting box 1 overcomes intermolecular forces; melting box 3 breaks covalent bonds.
The covalent bonds in box 1 are weaker than the covalent bonds in box 3, so they break at a lower temperature.
Box 1 has fewer atoms in the drawing than box 3, so less energy is needed to melt each gram of it.
Box 3 contains ions that attract each other strongly through ionic bonds, while box 1 contains neutral atoms that attract each other far less.

items.q: Struck with a hammer, the solid in box 2 shatters. Which explanation is correct?
options: Shifting a layer puts like charges side by side, and they repel.
The delocalized electrons are knocked loose, so nothing holds the cations together.
The intermolecular forces between its molecules are too weak to hold the solid in one piece.
Its covalent bonds are rigid and do not bend, so they snap like twigs when the crystal is struck with a hammer.

items.q: Dry ice, CO₂(s), turns to gas at −78 °C, while quartz, SiO₂(s), melts near 1,710 °C. Which statement explains the difference?
options: Solid CO₂ is molecules held by dispersion forces; quartz is a Si–O covalent network.
Si–O bonds are polar while C=O bonds are not, so quartz molecules attract each other more strongly.
Quartz molecules are heavier than CO₂ molecules, so they need more energy to leave the solid.
Quartz is an ionic solid made of Si⁴⁺ and O²⁻ ions, while CO₂ is made of neutral molecules.

items.q: What holds the particles of a molecular solid to each other?
options: Intermolecular forces
Covalent bonds throughout
Ionic bonds
A sea of electrons

items.q: Graphite and diamond are both pure carbon, yet graphite conducts along its layers and diamond does not. Why?
options: In graphite each C bonds to three others and one electron per C is delocalized; in diamond all four are in bonds.
Graphite contains carbon ions, while diamond contains neutral carbon atoms, so graphite has charge carriers.
Diamond's carbon atoms are held by weak intermolecular forces that block the movement of electrons.
Graphite is a metal, because carbon atoms arranged in layers give up their outer electrons the way metal atoms do.

items.q: A clear solid softens gradually from 550 °C to 700 °C instead of melting at one temperature. What does this best suggest?
options: It is an amorphous solid, with no long-range order.
It is a crystalline molecular solid whose molecules melt together at one time.
It is an ionic solid whose ions are beginning to conduct electricity.
It is impure, because a pure crystalline solid has no melting point.

items.q: Put these solids in order of melting point, lowest first.
options: Solid CH₄ (methane)
Ice, H₂O
Sodium chloride, NaCl
Diamond, C

items.q: Which substances form molecular solids? Select all that apply.
options: Sucrose, C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁
Silicon carbide, SiC
Potassium bromide, KBr
Solid carbon dioxide, CO₂
Copper, Cu

items.q: Naphthalene (C₁₀H₈, melts at 80 °C) and urea (CO(NH₂)₂, melts at 133 °C) are both molecular solids. Urea's molar mass (60.06 g/mol) is less than half of naphthalene's (128.17 g/mol). Which claim best explains urea's higher melting point?
options: Urea molecules hydrogen-bond through their N–H groups; naphthalene cannot.
Urea is a covalent network solid, so melting it breaks covalent bonds between the molecules in the crystal.
Urea molecules have more electrons than naphthalene molecules, so their dispersion forces are stronger.
Urea is ionic because it contains nitrogen, so its melting point lies between those of salts and molecules.

items.q: A student claims: "Ice melts at 0 °C because the O–H bonds in water break at that temperature." Which is the best correction?
options: Melting overcomes hydrogen bonds between molecules; the O–H bonds stay intact.
Ice melts because its ionic bonds break, releasing H⁺ and OH⁻ ions into the liquid that forms.
The claim is correct for ice, because ice is a covalent network solid of O–H bonds.
Ice melts because its dispersion forces break, while the hydrogen bonds stay intact in liquid water.

items.q: Which liquid has the strongest intermolecular forces?
options: Diethyl ether
Ethanol
Water
The three are about equal

items.q: From the graph, what is the normal boiling point of diethyl ether, in °C?

mistakes.why: Value: 20 °C is where ether's vapor pressure is 442 torr. The normal boiling point is where it reaches 760 torr.

items.q: On a mountain the air pressure is 355 torr. At about what temperature would water boil there?
Which statement best explains why ethanol's vapor pressure is higher than water's at 40 °C?
options: Ethanol molecules attract each other less strongly, so more of them escape the surface.
Ethanol molecules are heavier than water molecules, so they move faster and escape.
Ethanol has no hydrogen bonds, while water has strong ones between its molecules.
Ethanol's covalent bonds break at a lower temperature, producing more gas particles.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes all three curves?
options: Vapor pressure rises with temperature, and it rises faster at higher temperatures.
Vapor pressure rises by the same number of torr for each 10 °C increase in temperature.
Vapor pressure is zero below 20 °C, so the liquids do not evaporate in a cold room.
Vapor pressure rises with temperature until it reaches 760 torr, then it stays constant.

items.q: Which box shows the substance as a liquid?
options: P
Q
R
Q and R both

items.q: Which change is shown going from box Q to box P?
options: Sublimation
Melting
Condensation
Deposition

items.q: Why can the sample in box P be compressed into a much smaller volume, while the samples in Q and R can hardly be compressed?
options: In P the molecules are far apart; in Q and R they already touch.
The molecules in P are smaller than the molecules in Q and R, so more of them fit in a space.
The molecules in P have no attractions to each other, while those in Q and R are bonded together covalently.
The molecules in P are moving slowly, so they are easy to push closer, while those in Q and R move fast.

items.q: When the substance changes from box R to box P, what happens to its molecules?
options: Attractions between molecules are overcome; each molecule stays intact.
Covalent bonds within each molecule break and the atoms separate.
The molecules expand to fill the larger volume they now occupy.
New attractions form between the molecules, releasing energy.

items.q: A barometer reads 742 torr. What is this pressure in atmospheres?

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied by 760. Torr cancels only when 760 torr is on the bottom of the conversion factor.
Value: you divided by 101.325, the kPa-to-atm factor. For torr, use 760 torr = 1 atm.

items.q: A tire gauge reads 2.35 atm. What is this pressure in kilopascals?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided by 101.325. To go from atm to kPa, multiply: there are 101.325 kPa in each atm.
Value: you used 760, the torr conversion. 1 atm = 101.325 kPa.

items.q: Water sits in a sealed flask at 25 °C with liquid and vapor at equilibrium. Predict how the vapor pressure changes after each change, once equilibrium is restored.

variables.name: Move all of it, still at 25 °C, into a larger sealed flask with liquid left over

items.q: A student says, "Water at 25 °C has no vapor pressure because it is below its boiling point." Which is the best correction?
options: Some surface molecules escape at any temperature; water's vapor pressure at 25 °C is 23.8 torr.
Water has a vapor pressure at 25 °C once it has first been heated to 100 °C and then cooled back down.
The statement is correct; evaporation below the boiling point comes from dissolved air, not from water.
Water at 25 °C has a vapor pressure of 760 torr, the same as at its boiling point.

items.q: Pentane (C₅H₁₂) and hexane (C₆H₁₄) are both nonpolar. At 25 °C, which has the higher vapor pressure, and why?
options: Pentane, because fewer electrons give weaker dispersion forces.
Hexane, because its heavier molecules move faster and escape the surface of the liquid more often.
Pentane, because it can form hydrogen bonds that pull its molecules up and out of the liquid.
They are the same, because both are nonpolar and so neither one has attractions between its molecules.

items.q: What is a liquid's normal boiling point?
options: The temperature at which its vapor pressure equals 1 atm
The temperature at which it first starts to evaporate
The temperature at which its vapor pressure is zero
The highest temperature the liquid can ever reach

items.q: Which phase changes require energy to be added to the substance? Select all that apply.
options: Melting
Condensation
Sublimation
Freezing
Evaporation
Deposition

items.q: Two sealed flasks hold liquid bromine (Br₂) and liquid water at the same temperature, 20 °C. Bromine's vapor pressure is 175 torr and water's is 17.5 torr, yet a Br₂ molecule has about nine times the mass of an H₂O molecule. Which claim best fits the data?
options: Water molecules attract more strongly: they hydrogen-bond, while Br₂ has dispersion forces alone.
The data are wrong, because heavier molecules have lower vapor pressures than lighter ones.
Bromine molecules move faster than water molecules at the same temperature, because they are heavier.
Bromine's Br–Br bonds break easily, so the flask fills with Br atoms, which raises the pressure.

items.q: Water and its vapor are at equilibrium in a sealed flask at 25 °C. Which changes would raise the vapor pressure of the water? Select all that apply.
options: Raising the temperature to 35 °C
Adding more liquid water at 25 °C
Moving the water to a larger sealed flask at 25 °C
Adding nitrogen gas to the flask at 25 °C

items.q: How many moles of vapor filled the flask?

mistakes.why: Value: you used the temperature in °C. Gas laws need kelvin: 98.6 + 273.15 = 371.75 K.
Value: you used the pressure in torr with R in L·atm/(mol·K). Convert to atm first: 742.0 / 760.
Value: you used the volume in mL. R in L·atm/(mol·K) needs liters: 248.0 mL = 0.2480 L.
Value: you used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). With atm and liters, use R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K).

items.q: What is the molar mass of the unknown liquid, in g/mol?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided moles by mass. Molar mass is grams per mole: mass ÷ moles.
Value: this comes from using the temperature in °C. Convert to kelvin first.

items.q: Some water from the bath was left on the outside of the flask when it was weighed, but the student did not notice. How does this affect the calculated molar mass?
options: Too high, because the measured mass of vapor is too large while the calculated moles are unchanged.
Too low, because extra liquid on the outside means the flask held fewer moles of vapor than it did.
No effect, because the volume, temperature and pressure used to find moles were measured correctly.
Too high, because the extra water raises the calculated number of moles of vapor in the flask.

items.q: The unknown is either ethanol (46.07 g/mol), acetone (58.08 g/mol) or hexane (86.18 g/mol). Which is it, and on what evidence?

items.q: What is the total pressure in the container, in atm?

mistakes.why: Value: you used 27.0 °C. Convert to kelvin: 27.0 + 273.15 = 300.15 K.
Value: you used R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). For atm and liters, R = 0.08206 L·atm/(mol·K).

items.q: What is the partial pressure of O₂, in atm?

mistakes.why: Value: you split the pressure equally among three gases. Each gas's share follows its mole fraction, not the number of gases.

items.q: The temperature is raised to 87.0 °C, with the volume fixed. What happens to the mole fraction of O₂ and its partial pressure?

Both the mole fraction and the partial pressure increase.

items.q: 0.0500 mol of He is now pumped into the same container at 27.0 °C. What happens to the partial pressure of N₂?
options: It stays the same, because the moles of N₂, the volume and the temperature have not changed.

options: Pressure is directly proportional to kelvin temperature.
Pressure is inversely proportional to kelvin temperature.

items.q: If the same data were plotted against Celsius temperature, what would the graph look like?
options: A straight line that reaches zero pressure at −273 °C, not at 0 °C.

A horizontal line, because Celsius temperatures do not affect pressure.

items.q: The experiment is repeated with 0.200 mol of the same gas in the same container. How would the new line compare?

items.q: A 2.50 L sample of gas at 1.00 atm and 25.0 °C is compressed and heated to 3.20 atm and 75.0 °C. What is its new volume?

mistakes.why: Value: you used °C. The ratio 75.0/25.0 triples the volume; in kelvin the ratio is 348.15/298.15.
Value: you inverted the pressure ratio. Higher pressure makes the volume smaller: multiply by P₁/P₂.

mistakes.why: Value: you multiplied by 22.4 L/mol. Liters ÷ (liters per mole) gives moles.

items.q: A gas has a density of 1.96 g/L at 0.0 °C and 1.00 atm. What is its molar mass?

mistakes.why: Value: you calculated dP/RT. Rearranging PV = (m/M)RT gives M = dRT/P.

items.q: What volume does 16.0 g of methane, CH₄ (16.04 g/mol), occupy at 745 torr and 30.0 °C?

mistakes.why: Value: you used 745 torr with R in L·atm/(mol·K). Convert to atm: 745 ÷ 760.
Value: you used 30.0 °C. Convert to kelvin: 303.15 K.

items.q: Equal volumes of H₂ and CO₂ are at the same temperature and pressure. Which statement is true?

They have equal masses, but the H₂ sample contains more molecules.

They contain equal masses and equal numbers of molecules.

items.q: Put the steps for finding the moles of gas in a container in order.

Calculate n, keeping extra digits
Round n once, to the fewest significant figures in the data

items.q: Compared with sample X, what does sample Z's curve show about its temperature?

items.q: Samples X and Y are both at 300 K. Which statement about their particles is correct?

items.q: Why are the areas under the three curves equal?

The areas are equal because each gas has the same average speed.

items.q: Box 1 is heated until its particles match those in box 2. Which assumption of the kinetic molecular theory connects the change in speed to the change in temperature?

items.q: Box 2 is now squeezed to half its volume at constant temperature. What happens to the average speed of its particles, and to the pressure?
options: The average speed is unchanged and the pressure doubles.

The average speed is unchanged and the pressure is unchanged.

items.q: Which is an assumption of the kinetic molecular theory for an ideal gas?
options: Gas particles do not attract or repel each other.
Gas particles lose energy in each collision with a wall.
Gas particles take up most of the volume of the container.

items.q: A sealed, rigid can of gas is heated. Which particle-level explanation accounts for the rise in pressure?
options: The particles move faster, so they hit the walls more often and harder.
The particles expand as they warm, so they push harder on the walls.
More particles form as the heat breaks the gas into smaller pieces.

items.q: At 25 °C, by what factor is the average speed of H₂ (2.016 g/mol) greater than that of CO₂ (44.01 g/mol)?

items.q: A gas is heated from 27 °C to 177 °C. By what factor does the average kinetic energy of its particles increase?

mistakes.why: Value: you divided the Celsius temperatures. Kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature: 450.15 K / 300.15 K.
Value: that is the factor for the speed. Kinetic energy itself is proportional to T, so the factor is 450.15/300.15.

items.q: A student says: "When a gas is heated from 10 °C to 20 °C, the average kinetic energy of its particles doubles." What is wrong?
options: Kinetic energy is proportional to kelvin temperature, and 283 K to 293 K is a rise of only about 3.5%.
Heating a gas leaves the kinetic energy unchanged; it increases the potential energy of the particles.
The kinetic energy is halved, because hotter particles spread out and collide with each other less.

items.q: Which changes shift a gas's Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution toward higher speeds? Select all that apply.

Adding more of the same gas at the same temperature

items.q: Containers of He and of Ar have the same volume, temperature and number of atoms. Ar atoms are about ten times heavier and hit the walls harder. Why are the two pressures nonetheless equal?
options: The lighter He atoms move faster, so they hit the walls more often, which makes up for each hit being gentler.
The heavier Ar atoms move faster, so they hit the walls both more often and harder than the He atoms do.

items.q: Which statement about a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution is correct?
options: A few particles move much faster than the most probable speed, giving the curve a long tail.
Each particle in the sample moves at the speed marked by the peak of the curve.
The curve is symmetric, so as many particles are faster than the peak speed as slower.

CO₂ molecules take up the most volume, which lowers the measured pressure below the ideal value.

Ammonia behaves ideally, because the measured pressure is within a few atm of the ideal pressure.

items.q: The same 2.000 mol of gas at 450.0 K is put in a 100.0 L tank instead. How would PV/nRT for the ammonia compare with the value in the 1.000 L cylinder?

The same, because PV/nRT depends on the kind of gas and not on the conditions.
